description: TRAKATRA is a tech team from Bucaramanga, Colombia. Inspired by the leopard's speed, we process NASA’s SPHEREx infrared data with software engineering. We build an interactive tool analyzing thermal signatures to detect faint objects at the edge of our solar system—like Planet X—and explore the early universe.

Project Name Solar Shield

High-Level Project Summary Solar Shield is a free browser game that puts kids aged 7 to 12 in command of a base in Jezero crater on Mars. They fly a satellite, choose a landing site, place modules and balance power, life support and shielding, where every choice helps one meter and costs another. Then a real solar storm from May 2024 arrives, with its NASA DONKI record and the radiation rise that the Curiosity rover measured on Mars. Expert crew members disagree, and Iris, the base AI, is scrambled by radiation and starts giving wrong numbers. Kids learn what astronauts practice: read the instruments, weigh the advice, and verify before trusting a machine. No download, no account, in English and Spanish.

Link to Project Demo [Paste YouTube URL here]

YouTube Video Description Solar Shield is a browser game for ages 7–12, built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 ("Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer"). All gameplay shown is real screen capture of https://hackaton-nasa.trakatra.lat. Space-weather and radiation data are real, curated and static (NASA CCMC DONKI; NASA OSDR RadLab, RAD on Curiosity; NASA Mars Trek) — not live. Unofficial project, not endorsed by NASA.

Link to Final Projecthttps://hackaton-nasa.trakatra.lat

Repository Link (if requested)https://github.com/Joserraldo/nasa-space-apps-2026

Detailed Project Description What it does. Solar Shield puts a child in charge of an outpost at Jezero crater on Mars. There are three resources: power, life support (air, water, food) and shielding. Every action helps one meter and costs another, so no choice is free.

How it works. The child flies a satellite around Mars with limited battery, signal and shield, chooses a landing site among candidate sites in Jezero (each scored on three criteria; none wins them all) and places base modules. Then a storm arrives with its true NASA event ID and date. The game pauses and shows a source card: which dataset, which event, when it was downloaded. The storm of 20 May 2024 is the one the RAD instrument on the Curiosity rover measured on the Martian surface: that day its daily average was about 19 times higher than on a normal day (4.1 to 79.7 µGy/h, detector units).

The child consults a crew of original expert characters named by their role: an Engineer, a Radiation Doctor and a Space Weather expert. The experts sometimes disagree, and that disagreement is the trade-off. They are ordinary code that reads the game state and the curated data and answers with prepared sentences, so no number is ever invented.

Iris, the base AI, guides the child. Radiation damages electronics, so Iris starts to make mistakes, such as reporting a number that does not match the gauge. Her mistakes are scripted by rules, so the lesson is controlled: check the instruments and know whom to trust when technology fails. The child then sends a report to Earth and waits through the Mars–Earth message delay (about 3 to 22 minutes one way, computed from NASA NSSDC distances and the speed of light; shortened in play).

Failing never ends in a plain "Game over": the child sees a chain of causes (what was a decision, what was bad luck) and a science card.

Audience and benefits. Children aged 7 to 12, at home or in class. Simple words, terms explained in context, English and Spanish from the same build. The game trains trade-off thinking, reading instruments, comparing conflicting expert advice, and healthy skepticism toward automated systems.

Scientific foundation and NASA data. NASA CCMC DONKI gives the real storm events (IDs, dates). NASA OSDR RadLab gives the radiation actually measured by RAD on Curiosity. NASA Mars Trek gives real elevation and imagery of Jezero; slope, sunlight and shielding scores are derived by us and labeled as derived. NASA NSSDC gives Mars facts and distances. NASA OSDR studies feed the end-of-game science cards. All data are real, curated and static (downloaded 13–15 November 2026) and are never presented as live. Units are kept honest: µGy/h for the detector, mSv/day for people, never converted into each other. Non-NASA sources (Zhang et al. 2020, Chang'e-4; Canadian Space Agency) are credited as such.

How it addresses the challenge. Real decisions about life support, radiation shielding, power budgeting and communication delay; consequences tied to real space weather; language for ages 7–12; safe failure with explained causes; source credits inside the game.

Technology. TypeScript throughout. A pure TypeScript game engine that runs in the browser; React and Vite for the interface; Three.js for the procedural 3D scene (no external 3D models); Zod for data validation; Vitest unit tests and Playwright end-to-end tests; hosted on Cloudflare. No installation and no account: it opens from a link in a modern web browser. The layout is responsive and the 3D base has on-screen touch controls; we checked it in emulated desktop, tablet and phone viewports in both orientations (emulation, not a physical device lab).

Creativity. The twist is that the helpful AI is the thing that fails. Instead of teaching children to obey the computer, the game teaches them to verify it against instruments and human experts — using a storm that really happened.

Limits of this version (stated honestly). One playable mission (Mars, Jezero crater) with one fixed scenario. Data for four more missions (Moon near side, Moon south pole, Mars north pole, a surprise outpost) are curated but not playable. No voice input. The child's typed phrase is matched with keyword rules; no language model runs in the game.

Potential impact. A teacher can open one link on the devices a classroom already has and run a 15-minute session on space weather, risk and evidence, in two languages, with every number traceable to its source.

Unofficial project, not endorsed by NASA.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) We used AI coding agents (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, OpenCode) to write and review code, tests and documentation under human review; every merge was made by a human. AI assistants also helped draft and translate text. The game itself does not call an AI model at run time: the crew "experts" and the character Iris are rule-based code, and Iris's mistakes are scripted. No AI-generated content uses NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.

NASA Data NASA CCMC DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information) — https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/tools/DONKI/ — Real solar-storm events (CME, flare, SEP, geomagnetic storm) with their IDs and dates; the playable storm is CME 2024-05-20T05:36:00-CME-001. Curated, static.

NASA OSDR RadLab — https://visualization.osdr.nasa.gov/radlab/gui/data-api/ — Radiation measured by the RAD instrument on Curiosity on the Martian surface, in µGy/h; drives the storm's radiation rise. Curated, static.

NASA Mars Trek — https://trek.nasa.gov/mars/ — Elevation, shaded relief and imagery of Jezero crater for the landing sites; derived scores are labeled as derived.

NASA NSSDC Mars Fact Sheet — https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html — Earth–Mars distances, basis of the message delay. Seen in the playable path ("Earth's answer arrives in N turns").

NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) studies — https://osdr.nasa.gov/bio/repo/ — Science cards (food, bones, muscle, immune system, radiation), e.g. OSD-772. Bundled in the game's data package. The end screen shows "The real science behind it" cards with their sources.

Space Agency Partner Data and Other References Zhang et al. 2020, Science Advances (LND on Chang'e-4, CNSA) — https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aaz1334 — Reference dose for the Moon surface and the ISS comparison; credited as not NASA.

Reitz et al. 2016 (RAD / MSL) — https://elib.dlr.de/106090/ — Reference dose for people on the Mars surface, 0.64 mSv/day.

Canadian Space Agency (2026 Space Agency Partner) — https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/astronauts/living-in-space/eating-in-space.asp — Food cards curated for missions not yet playable; © CSA, credited as CSA.

NOAA SWPC — https://www.swpc.noaa.gov/ — Kp index values that appear inside DONKI storm records (Earth only).

React 18 — https://react.dev/ — User interface.

Vite — https://vite.dev/ — Build tool.

Three.js 0.160 — https://threejs.org/ — 3D scene.

Zod — https://zod.dev/ — Data validation.

Nunito (SIL OFL 1.1) — https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Nunito — Typeface.

Cloudflare Workers — https://workers.cloudflare.com/ — Hosting.

Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, OpenCode — https://claude.com/claude-code · https://openai.com/codex · https://opencode.ai/ — AI coding assistance.
